Contemned
kon-tĕmd'
v. (past tense of contemn: to despise, to hold in contempt, to reject with scorn; rendering Hebrew bazah, na'ats, and buz)
Latin contemnere, to despise, from con- intensive and temnere, to slight. The Authorized Version keeps the strong Latin verb where modern speech has only the noun contempt.

Biblical Definition

The word marks a settled judgment of the heart, not a passing insult. In the portrait of the man who shall abide in God's tabernacle, it is a mark of righteousness: “In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD” (Psa 15:4). The godly man's esteem runs by God's valuation and not the world's: he will not flatter a wicked man because he is powerful, nor despise a poor saint because he is obscure. Turned the other way, it is the sin of the wilderness generation: “they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High” (Psa 107:11), and the bondage and irons of that psalm are the consequence. Solomon uses it for the world's bargain with love: “if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned” (Son 8:7) — the offer itself would be despised, because love is not purchasable. Isaiah uses it of Moab's glory brought to nothing (Isa 16:14). Contempt, then, is a real and sometimes righteous act of the soul. Everything depends on what is being weighed and by whose scales.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to contemn as to despise; to consider and treat as mean and despicable; to reject with disdain; to slight; to neglect as unworthy of regard.

expand to see more

CONTEMN, v.t. To despise; to consider and treat as mean and despicable; to scorn.

2. To slight; to neglect as unworthy of regard; to reject with disdain.

CONTEMNED, pp. Despised; scorned; slighted; neglected; rejected with disdain.

Key Scripture

Psa 15:4 — "In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."

Psa 107:11 — "Because they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High:"

Son 8:7 — "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 15:4 is now read as a verse to be apologised for, because the modern conscience has been trained to believe that no man may be held in contempt for anything he does.

expand to see more

The fifteenth Psalm asks who shall abide in God's tabernacle and answers with a list of plain moral marks, one of which is that in his eyes a vile person is contemned. That clause is a genuine embarrassment to the modern conscience, and it is regularly softened into meaning nothing more than mild disapproval. Scripture means what it says: the man who walks with God does not honour wickedness, does not court it, does not seek the friendship of the vile because the vile is useful to him. And the psalm is careful to give the other half in the same breath — he honoureth them that fear the LORD. It is a matched pair, and both halves are about the same thing: whose estimate of a man do you take, God's or the world's? The corruption is not that people have grown too kind. It is that the valuation has been inverted. The same age that cannot bear to contemn a vile person has no difficulty at all contemning them that fear the LORD, and does it daily. Psalm 15 was never an invitation to be harsh. It was an invitation to weigh men on the only scales that will still be standing at the judgment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bazah (H959), to despise, to hold in contempt; na'ats (H5006), to spurn or reject with contempt; buz (H936), to hold in derision.

expand to see more

Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, to show contempt for; the same verb says of Christ that He was despised and rejected of men; Psalm 15:4, Isaiah 53:3.

Hebrew na'ats (H5006) — to spurn, to reject, to blaspheme; the wilderness sin against the counsel of the most High; Psalm 107:11, Numbers 14:11.

Hebrew buz (H936) — to hold in derision; the world's verdict on the man who would buy love with substance; Song of Solomon 8:7, Proverbs 6:30.

Usage

"“In whose eyes a vile person is contemned” — the man who values by God's scales and not the world's."

"“Contemned the counsel of the most High” — the wilderness sin, and the irons that followed it."

"“It would utterly be contemned” — love refuses to be bought, and despises the offer."
